newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa taps into first oil field.
newsitem.headline: South Africa taps into first oil field.

text.p: South Africa, traditionally reliant on local coal and imported crude oil to fuel its economy, will widen its energy base when the country's first oil field starts pumping in February.

At the historic naval base of Simon's Town, 700 workers are racing to refit a secondhand rig, which last saw service off the shore of Congo, and is now destined to bring in oil from the Oribi field in the stormy waters off South Africa's south coast.

Site manager Jon Hawkes said work on converting the rig to a floating production facility should be completed by mid-November, after which it will undergo sea trials before heading out to its final site 80 miles southwest of Mossel Bay. With an expected production rate of 20,000 barrels of oil
per day, the new field is a minnow by world standards -- but will supply some 5 percent of South Africa's current crude oil needs.

State-run oil firm Soekor and its 20 percent partner, Energy Africa Ltd., plan to pump the oil into a 1 million-barrel shuttle tanker for shipment to one of South Africa's three coastal refineries in Cape Town or Durban.
As a light crude, similar in quality to North Sea Brent, Oribi oil could trade at a premium.
However, industry sources said the limited local market and the fact that South African refineries are geared up to process heavier Middle East crudes may result in a sub-optimal price.
Nonetheless, Soekor is confident that the new field will pay its way easily, with capital costs being recovered during the first year of operation.

In contrast to the disastrous Mossgas plant, which processes gas into liquid fuel and ended up costing the government 11.4 billion rand ($2.5 billion), the development of offshore oil should not require South African taxpayers to dip into their pockets.
The $75 million needed for the project was raised earlier this year with syndicated loans, guaranteed by the government.

With probable recoverable reserves of 20 million barrels, Oribi -- previously known as E-BT -- would have a production life of four years, although the actual outcome could be anything between two and six years.

But Oribi is also expected to form the nucleus of a sequential development of several smaller fields in the Bredasdorp Basin, which should add extra recoverable reserves of 5 million to 40 million barrels, providing a further three to six years' life.

"There are six smaller fields adjacent to Oribi and the intention is that the production of the Oribi field is simply the first step towards a broader plan to produce these and other discoveries," said Hawkes.
Soekor has already earmarked the next field, E-AR, which will be brought on-stream and incorporated into the Oribi infrastructure as soon as capacity permits.
In addition, Hawkes said there were also several other promising nearby areas that might contain oil which Soekor aimed to drill in the next couple of years.
Compared with the rich oil pickings in West Africa and Angola, South Africa's oil reserves are thin, and international interest has been slow to emerge.

A government licensing round is still open since it was announced in 1993 but has not seen a single block awarded, something Soekor Chief Executive Joggie Heuser blames in part on the country's unattractive tax regime for high-risk fields.
Nonetheless, there are hopes the Oribi field might be the first of several small but profitable prospects.
Earlier this year, Phillips Petroleum signed a technical cooperation deal with Soekor giving it exclusive rights to evaluate blocks 17 and 18 off Durban.
